items.title: What Marx predicted
items.claim: Karl Marx predicted that capitalism would generate growing inequality and eventual crisis. Recent empirical work (Piketty, 2014) examined wealth concentration over centuries. What was a headline finding?

options.text: Wealth inequality has steadily fallen since 1800
When the rate of return on capital exceeds growth, wealth concentrates
Inequality is impossible to measure historically

items.reveal_title: r greater than g concentrates wealth
items.reveal:
Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2014) used tax records across France, UK, US and others to argue that when the return on capital (r) exceeds the economic growth rate (g), inherited wealth grows faster than earned income.

The book's data and conclusions remain contested but reopened debates Marx began.
items.why: Empirical historical economics revived classical sociological questions about class structure.

items.title: Merton's strain typology
items.claim: Robert Merton (1938) argued that crime arises when cultural goals exceed legitimate means. How many adaptations did he identify?
items.reveal:
Merton's 1938 essay 'Social Structure and Anomie' set out five responses to the gap between goals and means.

The theory has been extended by Agnew (1992) into General Strain Theory.
items.why: Strain theory still underpins much policy thinking about inequality and crime.

items.title: Willis's 'lads'
items.claim: Paul Willis's Learning to Labour (1977) studied working-class boys in a Midlands school. What did he argue they were doing through their counter-school culture?

options.text: Actively rejecting school in ways that prepared them for manual labour

items.reveal_title: Resistance that reproduced the very inequality it opposed
items.reveal:
Willis combined Marxist theory with ethnography to argue the 'lads' partially saw through school ideology but their rejection led them into the same factory jobs their fathers held.

The study influenced both education research and cultural studies.
items.why: Ethnographic fieldwork can reveal mechanisms of class reproduction invisible in statistics.
